messages.subject: sd() problem: sqrt(square(0))
parts:
We're getting nan's in sd() when all the elements are the same.

It's really coming from taking the sqrt of the square of 0. A minimal test case:

#include <stan/agrad/rev/sqrt.hpp>
#include <gtest/gtest.h>
#include <stan/agrad/var.hpp>

TEST(AgradRev,sqrt_square_zero) {
  stan::agrad::var x(0.0);
  stan::agrad::var f = sqrt(square(x));
 
  EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(0.0,f.val());
  std::vector<stan::agrad::var> g;
  g.push_back(x);
  std::vector<double> gradient;
  f.grad(g,gradient);
  EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(1.0,gradient[0]);
}

The gradient ends up being nan. By the way, this happens with multiplying x by itself as well. And if we change the function order.

The two chain methods (just the relevant pieces pulled out):

sqrt:
        void chain() {
          avi_->adj_ += adj_ / (2.0 * val_);
        }

square:
        void chain() {
          avi_->adj_ += adj_ * 2.0 * avi_->val_;
        }


In the test case outlined above, we start with the chain method in sqrt with:
avi_->adj_ = 0
adj_ = 1
avi_->val_ = inf
The resulting adjoint value is as expected: inf. (this seems reasonable in the limit as x approaches 0.)

Then we apply the chain rule and get into the chain method in sqrt with:
avi_->adj_ = 0
adj_ = inf
avi_->val_ = 0
The resulting adjoint value blows up: nan. This is from the inf * 2 * 0 condition. inf * 0 = nan.

The obvious right answer is d/dx sqrt(square(x)) = d/dx x = 1, but I can't figure out how to get there from local chain functions without some knowledge of the expression tree. An inf or 0 could arise in lots of ways, so it doesn't seem like creating a special case is the right thing to do.

So... what should we do?


Daniel

I can fix it. I worked out the analytic gradients,
which don't have this problem. That'll solve the
specific case of sd().

Not much we can do about general code that does sqrt(0)
but has some analytic reduction, like sqrt(square(x)) = x.
In general, there are lots of ways to express square(x), such
as x * x. And the case for sd() is more like sqrt(sum(square(x)).

I don't know how to do runtime type resolution, but we
might be able to catch the expression tree structure and
collapse it. But that doesn't solve the multiple ways
to express it problem.

- Bob

Didn't this issue come up a while back?

Mathematically, the derivative d/dx (sqrt(x)) is not well defined at x=0 so in some sense we can put whatever value we want because basically everything is wrong.  From a functional perspective, we never want to get a non-finite gradient out of the autodiff unless we absolutely must (e.g., someone divides by zero).  Putting those two things together, maybe we can just rewrite chain for sqrt() to be:

        void chain() {
          if (val_ > 1e-300)
avi_->adj_ += adj_ / (2.0 * val_);

else
              avi_->adj_ += adj_ / 2.0;
        }

or, alternatively,

        void chain() {
          avi_->adj_ += adj_ / (2.0 * std::max(val_,2e-300));
        }


Cheers,
Marcus

parts:
Returning a subgradient won't affect HMC at all except maybe on the level of efficiency but then only when there is significant mass at that region and even then I expect the impact to be small because we're returning something which will be close.  It's not "bad statistical mojo" as It certainly won't impact the statistical validity of our samples since a) the Metropolis test will use the same "correct" log prob and b) so long as the same subgradient is returned, the simulation will be reversible.  Patching the gradient is basically just using a different simulation Hamiltonian which is only different from the correct one in a small region around these gradient singularities.

If we throw an exception we're just going to reject everything and stop sampling in that region altogether.   Further, these rejections won't just occur at exactly x = 0, returning an unusually large gradient can overflow chain() calculations elsewhere resulting in a nan or inf gradient.

Regarding efficiency of patching the gradient vs throwing an exception, it's not clear which will be more efficient.  It seems to me allowing it to traverse through a region instead of automatically rejecting any trajectory which comes near the singularity would be more statistically efficient.

Here's the model (sd.stan):

}

>

That's our current implementation. We start there and end there. No indication that the sd() function is the one that's giving us grief.

Returning a subgradient won't affect HMC at all except maybe on the level of efficiency but then only when there is significant mass at that region and even then I expect the impact to be small because we're returning something which will be close.  

Unfortunately, we're artificially giving mass in these regions significant mass since we're initializing starting at 0.


That doesn't give the region mass.  If it has little real mass, sampling should quickly transition out of the region assuming that sampling can actually proceed.


Our problem lies with implementation. I agree with everything you've said in theory, but the implementation has initialization start in that region. We can't and don't get out. Stan just comes to a halt with an error message stating:
 
 
 
It's not "bad statistical mojo" as It certainly won't impact the statistical validity of our samples since a) the Metropolis test will use the same "correct" log prob and b) so long as the same subgradient is returned, the simulation will be reversible.  Patching the gradient is basically just using a different simulation Hamiltonian which is only different from the correct one in a small region around these gradient singularities.

If we throw an exception we're just going to reject everything and stop sampling in that region altogether.   Further, these rejections won't just occur at exactly x = 0, returning an unusually large gradient can overflow chain() calculations elsewhere resulting in a nan or inf gradient.

Regarding efficiency of patching the gradient vs throwing an exception, it's not clear which will be more efficient.  It seems to me allowing it to traverse through a region instead of automatically rejecting any trajectory which comes near the singularity would be more statistically efficient.

I'm in favor of catching errors early. One reason this was difficult to track down from the outside was due to the gradients going to nan without informative error messages. It was baffling because it only happened with sampling and not with optimization or test gradient mode. I believe we'll get a handle on the sqrt(square(0)) case soon, but the fundamental reason for this issue isn't going away and I'd like to be able to identify the problems much quicker.


Catching errors early is good but throwing exceptions is only useful if the caller is actually in a position to do something useful about it or there is no other resory.  In this case, all the caller can do is reject the sample and/or bail back to the user who is even less equipped to do something about it.


I'm assuming the error messages would bubble up past the caller all the way up to the user. Or at least to a developer that's trying to find issues with bad gradients.

 
 
Right now, I don't think we check gradients for nan values. Should we? It seems like a reasonable thing to do as opposed to what we currently do now, which is to integrate using nan derivatives and failing when the nans propagate to the positions. This could be done independent of error checking using exceptions.

We should definitely be checking gradients for non-finite values.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] sd() problem: sqrt(square(0))
parts:
On Wed, Nov 20, 2013 at 12:54 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
On Wed, Nov 20, 2013 at 12:48 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
If we change the gradient near singularities does it still get stuck?

No, it moves and samples just fine.
 
 Throwing an exception effectively punts the problem to the user.  I agree that we should be producing better error better error messages.

Yes, exactly. It's going to be difficult to hunt down every singular point. If users are alerted to a problem, if it's an actual problem with Stan code, I'm trusting that enough people will bring it to our attention. So yes, punting the problem to the user seems like the right thing to do.

But what's our response once it's been brought to our attention?  Should we work around it by patching gradients where reasonable?

Anyway, just to put a clear plan out there for us to discuss:

1) We should be checking gradients for non-finite values and reporting this as an error as soon as it's reasonable to detect.
2) Reporting more detailed error messages would be nice if we can find a way to do it without killing performance.  Perhaps we could have a compile-time option to check all adjoints after every individual chain() call.  This will be expensive, but will tell us precisely where our gradients go awry.  Alternatively we could add code to every chain() function but that's probably more work than simply hunting down every singular point.
3) When such errors are found and reported I think we should patch the gradients where it's reasonable to do so.  If the function itself is well defined at a point, we can generally come up with a reasonable subgradient which will allow sampling to proceed instead of simply punting the problem up the chain where there is less ability to do anything productive about it.

Basically all of the unconstrained parameters have been defined so that 0 inits should provide a reasonable starting point.  If a reasonable model (e.g., the double exponential) cannot be initialized at zero that seems like something we should fix as opposed to just saying it's a modelling mistake or requiring our users to jump through the massive hoops required for an explicit manual initialization.  I think this would be a somewhat different discussion if we had manual initialization block so we could just tell the user "change your initialization for this variable".

Cheers,
Marcus

parts:
I think this boils down to what we'd like to
see happen for the following calculation where
x and y are parameters:

mean <- (x + y) / 2;
var <- (pow(x-mean,2) + pow(y-mean,2)) / 2;
sd <- sqrt(var);

There's nothing wrong with the mathematical definition
and the variable sd has a finite analytic gradient w.r.t.
x and y.

The problem is that the current auto-diff's brute-force application
of the chain rule is going to kill the code on the sqrt(0)
if x == y.

We can write our own sd() with analytic gradients and solve
the problem for that case.

But the real issue is what to do for the above model?

As a side note, we should be promoting diagnose mode (test_grad
in RStan more heavily.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: definition of "variance"
parts: [pulled into its own thread for semantics mavens]

On 11/20/13, 1:50 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi, I'm confused. Var should divide by n-1, not by n.
> I'm not joking here, dividing by n-1 is the definition.

Sorry --- bad example. Stan absolutely divides by N-1
in the sd() and var() functions.

I'd go even further and separate four concepts that are
often just called "variance" in the literature:

1. variance (of a random variable or distribution)

2. population variance

3. sample variance

4. estimate of variance based on a sample

For (1), everyone divides by N for finite discrete random variables

For (2), Snedecor and Cochran (closest reliable book at hand) define
population variance as dividing by N.

For (3), Snedecor and Cochran define sample variance as dividing by N-1.

For (4), we know there are many estimators, the MLE (divide by N)
and unbiased (divide by N-1) being the usual pair in intro math
stats books. Arguably, a point estimate of variance should not
be called "variance", no matter how you define it.

Yet one more reason intro stat students (like I was only very very
recently and arguably still am) get really
really really confused from the standard presentations of this
material in intro courses and books and tutorials. For instance,
the R doc, always a source of enlightment, says simply:

This function computes the standard deviation of the values in x.

and later in the details section:

Like var this uses denominator n - 1.

The standard deviation of a zero-length vector (after removal of
NAs if na.rm = TRUE) is not defined and gives an error. The standard deviation
of a length-one vector is NA.
> We can have the convention that if n=1, we define variance to be 0.

We return the special NaN value rather than returning 0. We
treat it as 0 in n_eff calcs, though, I believe, so we don't get
all those NaN cases when a param doesn't move in a chain.

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] definition of "variance"
parts:
I'd set sd of a length 1 vector to the value 0. No point in having Nans running around, and I can easily envision examples where I might want to take sd in general cases that might include length 1 vectors.
The way it would work is that we might compute a weighted avg with a term such as (n-1)*sd. So the n-1 zeroes it out anyway. I don't think we should be giving out Nans when we can avoid it.

messages.subject: boundary conditions of sd() + doc
parts:
Sorry --- I keep confusing the 0 and 1 cases.
If size(x) == 0, then we raise an error. We could
have this case also return 0 and thus deal with the boundary
condition of empty bins in models.

In Stan 2.0.1, if size(x) == 1, then

sd(x) = var(x) = 0

and

d/dx_1 sd(x) = d/dx_1 var(x) = 0

Whatever we decide, I'll improve the doc in the manual to reflect
the boundary cases. We really need to do this for all of our functions,
as it's coming up a lot in user models. So expect about five
dozen of these discussions for everything from trig to Bessel
functions :-)

- Bob
